title: The overturning of the mandate in the Gokul Dairy cooperative is disturbing
content_html:
Amid a nationwide outcry over electoral malpractices, with fresh evidence emerging every day, the BJP government in Maharashtra has gone a step further in overturning a popular mandate through an executive fiat. It approved changing the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act through an ordinance on November 4 — which the Governor promulgated on November 6 — with the immediate effect of facilitating the takeover of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union, popularly known as Gokul Dairy, by the BJP and its allies. A Congress-led panel won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the board of the cooperative on October 19. Gokul, which is one of Maharashtra’s most influential cooperative institutions, has an annual turnover of around ₹4,000 crore and is linked to several lakh milk producers in western Maharashtra. The BJP had set its eyes on the cooperative sector as yet another arena of its political dominance, creating a Ministry of Cooperation under Home Minister Amit Shah. While that plan of controlling cooperatives continues to play out through various means, the overturning of an election clearly won by the Congress-led Opposition marks a new level of brazenness by the BJP, and of the impunity its actions continue to receive from the judiciary.

The Congress-backed Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi, led by Satej Patil, won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the Gokul board. On October 29, the election of the chairman was deadlocked after the BJP-allied members did not participate, and the meeting fell short of the required quorum of 14 members. The directors allied to the Congress and its partners subsequently declared Shashikant Patil Chuyekar as chairman, but the administration refused to recognise the election as quorum requirements had not been met. The amendment made through the ordinance allowed the government to nominate five directors to certain large cooperative institutions, with four nominees receiving voting rights. To be sure, four were nominated immediately to the Gokul board, and they voted with the BJP and its partners to elect a chairman on November 10. The mandate of the cooperative’s members had been 13-12 in favour of the Congress and its allies, but it turned 16-13 in favour of the BJP and its partners, with the appointment of members with voting rights by the State government. Those defeated approached the Bombay High Court on November 9 to restrain the government-nominated directors from voting, but the High Court did not grant that relief. The diffidence of the judiciary in intervening in favour of democratic principles is turning out to be a matter of concern. The overturning of the popular mandate in Gokul Dairy cannot be seen as an isolated incident. It is yet another instance in a troubling pattern of state power silencing the people’s choice.

title: This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society
content_html:
A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything, a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic, the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion. Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything, with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

title: How the algorithm is being targeted
author: Raviesha Pradeep
content_html:
On July 23, journalist Ila Kazmi posted a reel in which one could see a Delhi Police van at Jantar Mantar using facial recognition technology to match protesters’ faces in real time. By the next day, the reel was unavailable in India, and on September 9, her Instagram account was withheld. Instagram said that it was complying “with a legal request”. On October 9, the Delhi High Court in Ila Kazmi vs Union of India asked the Central government, Delhi Police, and Meta to produce the orders behind both blocks.

The Indian Express had reported that at least 25 people the police had allegedly placed as being at the protest were actually in jail at that time. In essence, a tool proven to err was implemented in a highly sensitive situation, and a video informing the public about the tool had been blocked. This is the condition of India’s present digital public square.

title: Reset tax on transfer of property
author: R.  Srinivasan,S.  Raja Sethu Durai
content_html:
Stamp duty and Registration Fees (SDR) are major components of States’ own-source tax revenue in India. In 2024-25, 11.7% of States’ own tax revenue was collected through SDR. Tamil Nadu is no exception, collecting 11.3% of its own tax revenue through this source. However, it has not harnessed this source to the same extent as Maharashtra and Karnataka, which collected 14.8% and 12.3% of their own tax revenues through SDRs, respectively. The Tamil Nadu government has recently constituted the Revenue Augmentation Committee to strengthen own-tax and non-tax revenues. The tax policies in other States should inform the Committee’s tax reforms.

SDRs are taxes imposed on the legal transfer of ownership of immovable property. Hence, they increase the property’s total effective cost. While SDRs are levied on the property’s value, the irony is that the property value is a function of the SDR. To resolve this, the State government fixes a guideline value and restricts registration of legal transfers below it. In practice, the actual value of the property being transferred is far above the guideline value. This can be addressed only through a scientific process of fixing guideline values and revising them periodically. At the same time, the SDR rate should encourage parties to declare the true value of the property being transferred.

title: Turning battery waste into strategic mineral wealth
author: Shyamasis Das
content_html:
In his concluding remarks at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 13, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi warned against the “weaponisation of technology and critical minerals”. His remarks assume significance amid rising global demand for critical minerals such as lithium, nickel and cobalt. As transport and other energy-intensive sectors increasingly shift towards electrification, the demand for electricity, lithium-ion batteries and electrical conductors is also growing.

Their ores are either scarce or their supply chains geographically concentrated, leaving these critical minerals vulnerable to geopolitical tensions, resource nationalism, trade restrictions and other disruptions. China currently dominates critical mineral processing. For India, which is heavily dependent on imports, securing reliable supplies has therefore become a strategic priority.

title: Letters to The Editor — November 12, 2026
content_html:
War and peace

It is a good augury that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. have begun in Abu Dhabi, raising hopes of ending the war that has been raging for nearly five years (Page 1, November 11). Both countries have suffered heavy losses of life and extensive damage to infrastructure. Even as talks are under way, attacks on each other continue. The participants are hopeful of reaching an agreement that will restore lasting peace in Europe. Both countries should earnestly pursue peace with a spirit of give and take, keeping the interests of their people in mind.

title: Tamil Nadu’s growing industrial water challenge
author: Rida Wanbha Nongbri,Yukesh  Saravanan
content_html:
Tamil Nadu is one of India’s leading investment destinations, thanks to its skilled workforce, strong manufacturing base and enterprise-friendly policies. Reflecting its investment-friendly credentials, NITI Aayog’s Investment Friendliness Index (IFI), released in July 2026, ranks the State third, behind Gujarat and Maharashtra. The first-of-its-kind report assesses States’ readiness to attract and sustain investments. For Tamil Nadu, it identifies limited international air connectivity, Chennai Port infrastructure constraints and inadequate industrial water supply in landlocked and rain-shadow districts as key lacunae.

Without compromising on water security, can Tamil Nadu expand its industrial base, albeit with a high MoU conversion rate, 22% better-than-average Air Quality Index score and strong disaster preparedness perception scores?
